description: Independent groups, repeated measures and matched pairs across lab, field and natural experiments.
content_html:
Why Use Experiments?

The experiment is the gold standard of psychological research. When a psychologist wants to establish that one thing causes another — not merely that the two are associated — an experiment is the method that can demonstrate causation. This is because experiments involve directly manipulating one variable while keeping everything else as constant as possible, then measuring the effect on another variable.

The key distinction the spec requires you to understand is between the research method (how the data is gathered) and the experimental design (how participants are allocated to conditions within the experiment). These are two separate decisions a researcher makes. A laboratory experiment can use any of the three experimental designs; so can a field experiment.

Key Fact

Research method = how data is collected (lab, field, natural experiment, observation, questionnaire etc.). Experimental design = how participants are divided between conditions (independent groups, repeated measures or matched pairs). These are distinct decisions — a common exam error is confusing the two.

Experimental Designs

Once a researcher decides to run an experiment, they must choose how to use their participants. There are three main experimental designs.

In an independent groups design, different participants take part in each condition. One group does condition A, a different group does condition B. For example, Group 1 revises with flashcards; Group 2 revises by rereading notes. They are separate, independent groups.

Strength: there are no order effects, because participants only experience one condition. Weakness: individual differences between the groups may affect results (one group might naturally have better memories), and more participants are needed because each person only provides data for one condition.

In a repeated measures design, the same participants take part in all conditions. Every person does condition A and condition B. This eliminates individual differences as a confounding variable, because the same person is compared to themselves.

Strength: individual differences are controlled — each participant acts as their own control. Fewer participants are needed. Weakness: order effects can occur. If participants do condition A first and then condition B, they may perform better on condition B because of practice (‘practice effect’), or worse due to fatigue or boredom. Counterbalancing (half the participants do A then B; the other half do B then A) can reduce order effects.

A matched pairs design pairs participants on a relevant variable (such as age, IQ or previous experience) before assigning one from each pair to each condition. It combines the advantages of independent groups (no order effects) and repeated measures (individual differences partly controlled).

Strength: individual differences are reduced because each pair is similar on the key variable; no order effects because each person only takes part in one condition. Weakness: very time-consuming to match participants carefully; impossible to match on every relevant variable; if one participant drops out, both members of the pair are lost.

Types of Experiment: Laboratory, Field and Natural

As well as choosing a design, a researcher must choose the setting and level of control. The three main types of experiment each involve the manipulation of an independent variable, but they differ in where they take place and how much control the researcher has.

A laboratory experiment takes place in a controlled setting, usually a specially designed room. The researcher can control many variables: lighting, noise, temperature, the exact stimuli presented and so on. Strength: high control means results more clearly reflect the IV; easier to replicate. Weakness: the artificial setting reduces ecological validity — participants may not behave as they would in everyday life.

A field experiment takes place in a real-world setting. The researcher still manipulates the IV but the participants are in their natural environment and may not know they are being studied. Strength: high ecological validity because behaviour occurs in a natural setting. Weakness: less control over extraneous variables; ethical concerns if participants have not consented.

A natural experiment involves a naturally occurring event as the IV — the researcher does not manipulate it but measures the effect of something that has happened independently. Strength: high ecological validity; allows study of variables that would be unethical to manipulate deliberately. Weakness: low control; participants cannot be randomly allocated to conditions because the IV was not chosen by the researcher.

Choosing the Right Design and Method

The choice of experimental design and research method depends on the research question. If a researcher is concerned about order effects and has enough participants, independent groups is the safest design. If individual differences are a major worry and order effects can be counterbalanced, repeated measures is preferable. If the research involves sensitive topics requiring real-world settings — for example, studying helping behaviour in a public space — a field experiment has advantages over a laboratory setting, even though it sacrifices some control.

Key Fact

Three experimental designs: independent groups (different participants per condition — no order effects but individual differences may confound); repeated measures (same participants, controls individual differences but risks order effects); matched pairs (paired on a variable, avoids order effects and reduces individual differences but time-consuming).
exam_tip_html: The most common error in research methods questions is confusing the research method with the experimental design. If a question asks you to ‘identify the experimental design’, the answer is independent groups, repeated measures or matched pairs — not ‘laboratory experiment’. If a question asks you to ‘identify the research method’, the answer is laboratory, field, natural experiment, observation etc. — not ‘independent groups’. Read the question carefully and answer what is actually asked.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Research method (lab, field, natural) and experimental design (independent groups, repeated measures, matched pairs) are distinct decisions. Confusing the two is one of the most common exam errors in research methods.
  • Independent groups use different participants per condition (no order effects, but individual differences may differ); repeated measures use the same participants (controls individual differences, but risks order effects); matched pairs pair participants to reduce differences without order effects.
  • Laboratory experiments offer high control but low ecological validity; field experiments offer higher ecological validity but lower control; natural experiments have no researcher manipulation of the IV.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes an independent groups design?
A) The same participants take part in all conditions
B) Participants are paired on a relevant variable before being assigned to conditions
C) Different participants take part in each condition
D) Participants are randomly assigned from the same group to different conditions, but some take part in both
practice_questions.marks: C) Different participants take part in each condition [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define what is meant by a 'natural experiment'.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 'An experiment in which the IV occurs naturally, rather than being manipulated by the researcher, who simply measures its effect.' — both elements present.
Secure: Core idea correct — states the IV is naturally occurring and the researcher measures it.
Developing: Mentions natural setting but misses that the IV is not manipulated by the researcher.
Emerging: Incorrect or incomplete definition.

practice_questions.text: Describe one strength and one weakness of a repeated measures design.
practice_questions.marks:
Strength: individual differences are controlled — the same participants take part in all conditions, so any differences between conditions reflect the IV rather than participant differences.
Weakness: order effects can occur — participants may perform better in the second condition due to practice, or worse due to fatigue.
Mastering: Both strength and weakness clearly described with reason.
Secure: Both identified, one described well.
Developing: One point, partially explained.
Emerging: One vague point.

practice_questions.text: A researcher wants to investigate whether people solve puzzles faster in silence or with music playing. She uses the same 20 participants in both conditions. Identify the experimental design and suggest one way to control for order effects.
practice_questions.marks:
Design: repeated measures (same participants in both conditions).
Order effects control: counterbalancing — half the participants do the silence condition first, then music; the other half do music first, then silence. This ensures any practice or fatigue effects are spread equally across both conditions rather than affecting one condition more than the other.
Mastering: Design correctly identified and counterbalancing explained with mechanism.
Secure: Design correct, counterbalancing mentioned but not fully explained.
Developing: Design correct only.
Emerging: Design incorrect or missing.

practice_questions.text: Describe the three main experimental designs used in psychological research.
practice_questions.marks:
Students should cover:
- Independent groups: different participants in each condition. Strength: no order effects. Weakness: individual differences may affect results.
- Repeated measures: same participants in all conditions. Strength: individual differences controlled. Weakness: order effects (practice, fatigue).
- Matched pairs: participants paired on a relevant variable, one per pair per condition. Strength: reduces individual differences without order effects. Weakness: time-consuming; perfect matching impossible.
Mastering: All three designs with at least one strength and one weakness each.
Secure: All three described, two with strength/weakness.
Developing: Two designs described.
Emerging: One design.

practice_questions.text: Describe and evaluate laboratory experiments and field experiments as methods used in psychology.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (AO1):
- Laboratory experiment: conducted in a controlled setting; researcher manipulates IV and controls extraneous variables closely.
- Field experiment: conducted in a real-world setting; researcher manipulates IV but participants are in their natural environment, sometimes without knowing they are being studied.

Evaluation (AO3):
- Lab strength: high control of extraneous variables; results more clearly show effect of IV; high replicability.
- Lab weakness: low ecological validity — artificial setting means participants may behave differently from everyday life (demand characteristics).
- Field strength: higher ecological validity because behaviour occurs in natural setting; reduces demand characteristics if participants are unaware.
- Field weakness: researcher has less control over extraneous variables; ethical issues if participants have not given informed consent.
- Comparison: choice between lab and field depends on whether internal validity (control) or ecological validity (real-world applicability) is more important for the research question.

Mastering: Both methods described accurately with elaborated evaluation including comparison.
Secure: Both described, evaluation present.
Developing: One method described well, one point of evaluation.
Emerging: One method, little evaluation.

knowledge_checks.q: Which experimental design uses the same participants in both conditions of an experiment?
A study is conducted in a laboratory with high researcher control. What is the main weakness of this research method?
options: It cannot establish cause and effect
The independent variable cannot be measured

knowledge_checks.q: In a _____ design, participants are paired on a relevant variable and one member of each pair is allocated to each condition.
The way in which data is collected (e.g. laboratory, field, observation) is called the research _____, which is distinct from experimental design.
Match each experimental design to its key feature:
right: Different participants in each condition — no order effects
Same participants in all conditions — controls individual differences
Paired on a variable — reduces differences without order effects

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key difference between a research method and an experimental design?
flashcard_questions.a: Method = how data is collected; design = how participants are allocated to conditions.

flashcard_questions.q: What is an independent groups design?
flashcard_questions.a: Different participants take part in each condition of the experiment.

flashcard_questions.q: What is one strength of an independent groups design?
flashcard_questions.a: No order effects because participants only take part in one condition.

flashcard_questions.q: What is one weakness of an independent groups design?
flashcard_questions.a: Individual differences between groups may affect results.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a repeated measures design?
flashcard_questions.a: The same participants take part in all conditions of the experiment.

flashcard_questions.q: What are order effects in a repeated measures design?
flashcard_questions.a: Performance changes due to practice (improvement) or fatigue (decline) from doing multiple conditions.

flashcard_questions.q: How does counterbalancing reduce order effects?
flashcard_questions.a: Half the participants do condition A then B; the other half do B then A, balancing out order effects.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a matched pairs design?
flashcard_questions.a: Participants are paired on a relevant variable, with one from each pair allocated to each condition.

flashcard_questions.q: What is one weakness of a matched pairs design?
flashcard_questions.a: Time-consuming to match participants; perfect matching on all relevant variables is impossible.
The IV occurs naturally rather than being manipulated by the researcher.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do laboratory experiments have low ecological validity?
flashcard_questions.a: The artificial setting means participants may not behave as they would in everyday life.

flashcard_questions.q: What is one strength of a field experiment over a laboratory experiment?
flashcard_questions.a: Higher ecological validity because behaviour occurs in a natural, real-world setting.

glossary_terms.definition: The way in which data is collected in a study, for example laboratory experiment, field experiment, observation or questionnaire.
The way in which participants are allocated to conditions within an experiment, for example independent groups, repeated measures or matched pairs.
An experimental design in which different participants are used in each condition of the experiment.
An experimental design in which the same participants take part in both (or all) conditions of the experiment.
An experimental design in which participants are paired on a relevant variable and then one member of each pair is placed in each condition.
An experiment conducted in a controlled, artificial environment where the researcher has a high degree of control over variables.
An experiment conducted in a real-world setting in which the researcher deliberately manipulates the independent variable.
An experiment in which the independent variable is naturally occurring rather than deliberately manipulated by the researcher.

hero_image_caption: Controlled laboratory settings allow psychologists to test cause-and-effect relationships.
